title: Turing Machine
body:
The top rung of the ladder in [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]], and the definition of
"computable" itself. A [[Finite Automata|finite automaton]] has no memory beyond its state.
A [[Pushdown Automata|pushdown automaton]] adds a [[Stack]], so it can count. A Turing
machine adds an unbounded tape it can read *and write*, and move over in both directions,
and that turns out to be enough to compute anything computable at all.

It is a deliberately terrible computer. Nobody would build one. The point is that it is
simple enough to reason about mathematically, and powerful enough that nothing else beats
it.

## The machine

A finite control (an ordinary state machine) plus an infinite tape divided into cells, plus
a head sitting over one cell. On each step the machine:

1. reads the symbol under the head,
2. writes a symbol to that cell, possibly the same one,
3. moves the head one cell left or right,
4. changes state.

That is the entire instruction set. The tape starts with the input written on it and blanks
everywhere else.

## Formal definition

A Turing machine is a 7-tuple $M = (Q, \Sigma, \Gamma, \delta, q_0, q_{accept}, q_{reject})$:

| Part | What it is |
|---|---|
| $Q$ | finite set of states |
| $\Sigma$ | input [[Alphabet]], which does not contain the blank symbol |
| $\Gamma$ | tape alphabet, where $\Sigma \subseteq \Gamma$ and the blank $\sqcup \in \Gamma$ |
| $\delta$ | transition function $Q \times \Gamma \to Q \times \Gamma \times \{L, R\}$ |
| $q_0$ | start state |
| $q_{accept}$, $q_{reject}$ | halting states, and they are distinct |

The shape of $\delta$ is the whole story. Compare it to a [[DFA]], whose transition function
is $Q \times \Sigma \to Q$: the DFA cannot write, cannot move backward, and cannot use any
memory outside $Q$.

## Halting, and the three outcomes

Run a Turing machine on an input and exactly one of three things happens:

- it reaches $q_{accept}$ and **accepts**,
- it reaches $q_{reject}$ and **rejects**,
- it never reaches either and **loops forever**.

That third outcome is not a design flaw, it is the source of everything interesting in the
course. It gives two different classes of language:

| Class | Also called | Requirement |
|---|---|---|
| **Recursively enumerable** | Turing-*recognisable* | Some TM accepts every string in $L$. On strings not in $L$ it may reject or may loop forever. |
| **Recursive** | *Decidable* | Some TM halts on **every** input, accepting strings in $L$ and rejecting the rest. |

Decidable is the strictly stronger property, and it is what "there is an [[Algorithm]] for
this" actually means.

> A language is decidable if and only if both it and its complement are recognisable.

## Variants that change nothing

All of these recognise exactly the same class of languages as the basic model:

- multiple tapes,
- a tape infinite in both directions,
- multiple tracks per tape,
- a nondeterministic machine (see [[Nondeterminism]]).

The nondeterministic case is worth pausing on, because for [[Finite Automata]] the same
result held ([[NFA]] and [[DFA]] are equivalent) but for [[Pushdown Automata]] it did *not*:
a nondeterministic PDA is strictly stronger than a deterministic one. For Turing machines
the equivalence comes back. A deterministic machine simulates a nondeterministic one by
searching its tree of configurations, which costs exponential *time* but no extra *power*.
That gap between power and time is exactly where [[NP-Complete]] lives.

## The universal Turing machine

A Turing machine can be written down as a string. So there is a machine $U$ that takes
$\langle M, w \rangle$, the description of a machine plus an input, and simulates $M$ on
$w$.

This is the stored-program idea, twelve years before hardware caught up with it, and it is
why [[VonNeumann]] architecture looks the way it does: a machine whose instructions live in
the same memory as its data. It is also what makes [[Undecidability]] possible, because a
machine can now be handed a description of itself.

## Church-Turing thesis

> Anything that can be computed by any effective procedure can be computed by a Turing
> machine.

It is a *thesis*, not a theorem. "Effective procedure" is an informal idea, so there is
nothing to prove against. The evidence is that every independent attempt at a definition has
landed in the same place: [[Lambda Calculus]], general recursive functions, register
machines, [[Cellular Automata]], and every real programming language all compute exactly the
same set of functions. A system powerful enough to simulate a Turing machine is called
**Turing complete**.

## The limits

Once you have a universal machine you can build a self-referential contradiction, and the
whole edge of computability falls out. See [[Undecidability]] for the argument in full:

- The **halting problem**, "does machine $M$ halt on input $w$?", is undecidable.
- The proof is a [[Proof By Contradiction]]. Assume a decider $H$ exists, build a machine
  $D$ that asks $H$ what $D$ itself does and then does the opposite, and ask what $D$ does
  on its own description. Both answers are wrong.
- $A_{TM}$, "does $M$ accept $w$?", is recognisable but not decidable. Just simulate $M$;
  if it accepts you find out, if it loops you wait forever.
- Most functions are not computable at all, by counting: there are countably many Turing
  machines and uncountably many functions from strings to $\{0,1\}$.
- The busy beaver function grows faster than any computable function.

The same self-reference drives [[Godel's Theorem]] in logic, and the two results are usually
taught as cousins.

## Where it sits

The [[Chomsky Hierarchy]] in one line:

$$\text{regular} \subset \text{context-free} \subset \text{context-sensitive} \subset \text{recursively enumerable}$$

recognised respectively by [[Finite Automata]], [[Pushdown Automata]], linear bounded
automata, and Turing machines. Each step up is a step up in memory, and each step is
*strict*: there is a language at every level that the level below cannot manage.

Turing machines are also the model in which [[Time Complexity]] is defined. "Polynomial
time" means polynomial in the number of TM steps, which is why the definition of P and NP
survives changing programming languages.

## Core Facts to Know

- A Turing machine is a finite control plus an unbounded read/write tape.
- The transition function is $\delta: Q \times \Gamma \to Q \times \Gamma \times \{L, R\}$.
- One step reads a symbol, writes a symbol, moves the head one cell, and changes state.
- $\Sigma$ is the input alphabet and never contains the blank; $\Gamma$ is the tape alphabet and does.
- A TM either accepts, rejects, or loops forever.
- **Recognisable** (recursively enumerable): some TM accepts every string in the language.
- **Decidable** (recursive): some TM halts on every input.
- Every decidable language is recognisable; the reverse is false.
- $L$ is decidable if and only if $L$ and its complement are both recognisable.
- Multi-tape, two-way-infinite-tape, and nondeterministic TMs all have the same power as the basic model.
- A nondeterministic TM can be simulated deterministically with exponential slowdown.
- Unlike with [[Pushdown Automata]], nondeterminism buys a TM no extra power.
- A **universal Turing machine** takes $\langle M, w \rangle$ and simulates $M$ on $w$.
- The universal TM is the stored-program idea, and the ancestor of [[VonNeumann]] architecture.
- The **Church-Turing thesis** says effectively computable means Turing computable.
- The thesis cannot be proved, because "effectively computable" is informal.
- **Turing complete** means able to simulate any Turing machine.
- [[Lambda Calculus]] is Turing complete and was developed independently.
- The **halting problem** is undecidable.
- The halting proof is [[Proof By Contradiction]] via self-reference and diagonalisation.
- $A_{TM}$ is recognisable but not decidable.
- Almost all functions are uncomputable: countably many machines, uncountably many functions.
- Turing machines recognise exactly the recursively enumerable languages, the top of the [[Chomsky Hierarchy]].
- P and NP are defined in terms of Turing machine steps, which is what makes them language-independent.
